title: Usage guide
description: Not sure which model to use? The overview compares them per task: commercial status, accuracy, speed against the original code and memory.
html:
Not sure which model to use? The overview compares them per task: commercial status, accuracy, speed against the original code and memory.

Install

From a git checkout: uv pip install -e '.[libs]' (or pip install -e '.[libs]'; a plain pip install . works too) installs every model plus timm, torchvision, transformers and ONNX ([libs]).

pip install fastforks installs everything: every model plus timm, torchvision, transformers and ONNX export. pip install fastforks-core is the lean install: the API and every model whose code licence is permissive, no optional libraries; its extras add the rest. fastforks-core[nc] adds the models with non-commercial or GPL code (S2M2, FoundationStereo, MonSter, CoEx, ...; see licences), fastforks-core[timm] / [torchvision] / [transformers] the libraries some families are built on, fastforks-core[onnx] ONNX export and fastforks-core[libs] all of those libraries; fastforks is fastforks-core[nc,libs]. TensorRT is a separate extra (fastforks-core[tensorrt], or fastforks[tensorrt]). A model whose library is missing fails in load with the pip command to run, before any weight is read. fastforks.model_card(id).requires (or the task's model_card) shows what a model needs and list_models(runnable=True) lists the models whose dependencies are installed and whose non-commercial opt-in is set; it does not check weight access (gated repos), downloads or the offline cache.

A release is the fastforks-core wheel with the permissive model code, the fastforks-nc wheel with the rest and the fastforks metapackage (no code), so fastforks-core never pulls non-commercial or GPL code.

Cache and environment variables

Weights and kernel binaries are downloaded on first use into the user cache (~/.cache/fastforks on Linux; the download line names the folder; fastforks env prints it with its size). It grows with every model you use; to free space delete the folder (fastforks download MODEL refetches). XDG_CACHE_HOME is honoured. Concurrent downloads of the same file are safe but not deduplicated. Path variables expand ~; relative paths resolve against the current directory.

variablemeaning
FASTFORKS_CACHEcache directory (default: the platform user cache)
FASTFORKS_WEIGHTS_PATHextra directories searched for weight files before downloading (os.pathsep-separated)
FASTFORKS_KERNEL_PATHextra directories searched for kernel binaries (offline machines, own builds)
FASTFORKS_OFFLINE1 = never touch the network (also HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1); missing files raise WeightsDownloadError
FASTFORKS_NONCOMMERCIAL1 = also download weights with non-commercial licences (off in every install, also fastforks)
FASTFORKS_COMMERCIAL_ONLY1 = refuse (and hide from list, download) every model not cleared for commercial use
FASTFORKS_HF_ENDPOINTredirects only our own Hugging Face repos (kernels, mirrored weights) to a mirror or file:// stand-in, not the authors' hosts; for a full mirror use FASTFORKS_WEIGHTS_PATH

The three on/off variables take 1/true/yes/on or 0/false/no/off/empty (any case); any other value raises OptionsError. mode and device are load arguments; there are no FASTFORKS_MODE / FASTFORKS_DEVICE variables. | HF_TOKEN | sent only to our own Hugging Face repos (private or rate-limited access); other repos: huggingface_hub's own login |

Quickstart per task

Every task works the same way: <task>.load(model_id) once, then call the model; <task>.list_models() (or fastforks.list_models() for all tasks, fastforks list on the command line) shows the installed ids.

Stereo matching (models, API):

from fastforks import stereo

model = stereo.load("igev-stereo-sceneflow")  # our kernels on a supported GPU, else portable PyTorch (GPU or CPU)
result = model("left.png", "right.png")
result.disparity  # [H, W] float32 tensor on the model's device, pixels at the input resolution (x_left - x_right)
result.backend  # what ran: Backend(mode='kernels', device='cuda:0', dtype='float16', kernels=(...))

Monocular depth (models, API):

from fastforks import depth

model = depth.load("depth-anything-v2-s")
result = model("room.jpg")  # metric models: model("room.jpg", intrinsics=K), K [3, 3] in pixels (see below)
result.inverse_depth  # [H, W] float32; result.kind says what the maps mean (here relative inverse depth)
result.backend

result.kind is metric (metres) or a relative kind (unknown scale or shift: da3mono-large, MiDaS, Depth Anything V2). Metric models differ in the camera: metric3d-vit-large and da3metric-large need the real intrinsics= for correct metres (da3metric-large: metres = output x focal / 300; without intrinsics= it assumes a 300 px focal length, which is too small for a real camera), unidepth-v2-vitl14, unik3d-vitl, depth-pro and MoGe estimate the camera (given intrinsics= replace fx) and return it as result.intrinsics, zoedepth-nk takes none. fastforks info MODEL shows kind.

Other tasks work the same way (families built on timm, torchvision or transformers need that extra):

# needs: pip install "fastforks-core[torchvision]"
from fastforks import classification, features, segmentation

classification.load("resnet50")("cat.jpg").top(3)  # [(class name, probability), ...]
segmentation.load("dinov2-s-linear-ade20k")("street.jpg").labels  # [H, W] class index per pixel
features.load("dinov2-vitb14")("cat.jpg").pooler_output  # image embedding; .last_hidden_state has all tokens

# needs: pip install "fastforks-core[torchvision]" "fastforks-core[nc]"
# MVSAnywhere's code and weights are non-commercial: its weights download only with FASTFORKS_NONCOMMERCIAL=1
from fastforks import detection, multiview, promptable_segmentation

det = detection.load("faster-rcnn-r50-fpn-3x-coco")
det("street.jpg", score_threshold=0.5).to_list()  # dicts: box, class_name, score
# defaults of every detection family: score >= 0.05, at most 100 boxes (load options score_threshold, max_detections)
# a batch gives list[DetectionResult] (one per image; the only task that returns a list, the others a batched result)
sam = promptable_segmentation.load("sam-vit-b")
# one point (x, y) in pixels, label 1 = foreground: masks [3, H, W] bool (3 candidates), iou_scores [3]
r = sam("cat.jpg", input_points=[[320, 240]], input_labels=[1])
best = r.masks[r.iou_scores.argmax()]  # [H, W]; several prompts add a leading axis; also input_boxes=, text= (SAM 3)
# SAM 3's text prompt cuts scores with threshold= (a call keyword only), detection with score_threshold=
multiview.load("mvsanywhere")(
    ["a.jpg", "b.jpg"], intrinsics=K, cam_to_world=poses
).depth  # [1, H, W]: the reference view (reference= picks it)

How a call runs: the model card (card.toml) is resolved to a variant (the id and revision); the variant and mode select a runner (portable or kernels backend) with its weights; the task API (<task>.load) wraps the runner and turns the input into tensors; calling it returns the typed result, whose .backend records what ran. The exceptions follow.

Each task has its own module: fastforks.stereo, fastforks.depth, fastforks.classification, fastforks.segmentation, fastforks.features, fastforks.detection, fastforks.promptable_segmentation and fastforks.multiview. multiview models differ in what they need: PatchmatchNet also takes depth_range=(near, far); MVSAnywhere and PatchmatchNet return the reference view only. See the API pages for every result's fields.

Every result has .to(device) and .cpu() (same type, so save, top, ... keep working; tensors already there are not copied), and .numpy() for a dict of arrays.

Load once, call many times: weights and (for kernels) kernels are loaded by load, so a call only runs the network. The rest of this guide uses stereo in its examples; everything applies to every task.

Calibrated stereo in one call

Raw (unrectified, possibly distorted) pairs with a calibration go in as they are; rig= takes a calibration file (any format of read_calib) or a StereoRig you built:

from fastforks import stereo

model = stereo.load("fast-acvnet-generalization")
result = model("left.png", "right.png", rig="calib.yaml")  # rectify -> match -> back to the left image
result.depth()  # [H, W] metres at the left image's pixels, NaN where no source pixel exists
result.valid()  # the mask of depth(): [H, W] at the left image's pixels
depth = result.depth().cpu().numpy()  # depth() / valid() are torch tensors on the model's device
result.save("scene.ply")  # point cloud in the left camera's frame, coloured by the left image
  • result.depth(euclidean=False), .points(frame="camera"), .disparity, .confidence and .extras belong to the main view; euclidean=True returns the distance along each pixel's ray instead of the depth z. views="right" or "both" also runs the right camera; result.left and result.right are the per-view results with the same methods (each in its own camera frame), and result.view names the main one (the left for "both"). The views run one after the other and share the decoded images, the rectification maps and the compiled plans. A view that was not run raises InputError. Batches ([B, 3, H, W]) give [B, H, W] maps.
  • fastforks.save(path, thing) writes a result, a PointCloud or an [H, W] map; the suffix selects the format (.tif, .npy, .pfm, .ply, .las / .laz for clouds). result.save(path, key=None) and result.right.save(...) are the shortcuts for a result; .png (KITTI 16-bit disparity) only through a stereo result's save.
  • size=(height, width) and focal= set the rectified image (default: the input size and the left camera's fx; the principal point is the image centre), the same as g.rectify(rig).
  • Holes (no source pixel, invalid disparity) are NaN everywhere.
  • Two pixel grids: depth() and valid() are at the original (input) pixels; disparity, confidence, extras and points() are on the rectified grid (size=). Mask those with valid(grid="rectified") (or cloud.valid), not valid(). Without rig or with a RectifiedRig the grids are the same.
  • depth() is cached; numpy() (and run_many's numpy maps) are read-only arrays, so an edit cannot leave the cache stale: .copy() to edit. The shared Rectification's matrices are read-only too.
  • The maps are built once per (calibration, size, device) and cached, so a second call only runs the network; a plain model(left, right) is unchanged.
  • model.run_many(lefts, rights, rig=..., views=..., size=..., focal=...) applies the calibration to every pair; with save_to= the right view is saved as <name>_right<suffix>.
  • Directory inputs (run_many, stereo run) are not recursive (use a glob such as 'dir/**/*.jpg'); an unreadable entry or broken symlink is a failed pair (--skip-errors reports it and the command exits 1).
  • Several rigs: load the model once in Python and call run_many once per calibration.

Already rectified pairs (Middlebury, KITTI) work the same: rig=read_calib("calib.txt") (a RectifiedRig, see calibration files), then result.depth().

Principal points follow OpenCV: pixel centres at integer coordinates, image centre ((W - 1) / 2, (H - 1) / 2); resizing uses c' = (c + 0.5) s - 0.5 and COLMAP's cx is read as cx - 0.5.

Process-global state: CUDA and MPS calls of all models run one at a time per process (see Threads); kernels runs on one CUDA device per process (a second device raises BackendUnavailableError: use one process per GPU); and load temporarily sets torch.get_default_dtype() to float32 and patches the torch.nn.init initialisers while it builds the network (restored afterwards, but visible to other threads running at that moment).

Choosing a backend: mode

Four things differ and are reported separately: a model is installed when its package and card are present (fastforks list); its dependencies are available when the optional libraries it needs (timm, transformers, torchvision, ... ; runnable=True in list_models) are present, else load raises; a backend is supported when the card lists the mode and this device and architecture fit it (kernels: see platforms); and a model is validated when golden parity against the reference code is recorded (the "Parity" rows of the model pages).

moderuns onwhat you get
"portable"CPU, CUDA, Apple silicon (MPS), other PyTorch devices where the network's ops existthe original network in plain PyTorch, checked against the reference
"kernels" (CUDA)NVIDIA GPU, compute capability >= 8.0, driver >= 570our CUDA kernels, faster than portable (benchmarks per model); memory is similar, sometimes higher. Raises BackendUnavailableError (its subclass KernelUnavailableError for a missing GPU or binary) with the reason if it cannot run here; never falls back silently
"kernels" (Metal)Apple silicon, macOS, the families listed under Apple siliconMetal kernels, compiled on the device on first use; same error behaviour
"auto" (default)anywherekernels if it can run and the recorded measurements prefer it for this model, else portable (a few plain ViT classifiers gain nothing from kernels); the choice is logged once per load (WARNING if kernels fails on a CUDA device, else INFO) and recorded in result.backend

mode selects the backend; the result's result.backend (and .mode) reports which one ran.

fastforks bench MODEL times all of this on your machine (see below).

Compute dtype: dtype

  • None (default): the model's tested precision (fastforks info MODEL): float16 / bfloat16 on CUDA where the model supports it, float32 on the CPU and on Apple MPS, always reduced precision for kernels.
  • "float32": float32 everywhere, portable only (kernels raises OptionsError). This is the reference-accurate path: the closest to the original implementation, slower and with more memory. CUDA convolutions then use PyTorch's default TF32; torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False makes them full float32 and the output CPU-identical (slower: HITNet 720x1280 70 -> 230 ms).
  • "float16" / "bfloat16": need CUDA and a dtype the model code implements (portable) or the kernels' own dtype (kernels; mode="auto" then falls back to portable), or MPS where the card lists float16 (see below); anything else raises OptionsError naming the dtypes available. A dtype other than the tested one is logged and not covered by the reference checks.

Precision of kernels (CUDA): the card's kernels dtype (float16; bfloat16 for one family; see the table); some heads and box / mask steps stay float32 (noted on the card). Families that list cudnn_hacc also accumulate convolutions in float16: faster on GeForce, a larger error than portable float16. Each family's GPU golden tolerances ("Parity" on the model pages) bound the error. On MPS the Metal kernels run float16 for stereo and float32 for MoGe-3 and VGGT.

Every model is checked against reference outputs: saved results of the original code at a pinned commit, which the portable (CPU, float32) and CUDA backends must match. fastforks info MODEL shows the pinned commit. "<id>@N" is an assertion against revision drift: it checks that the installed package has revision N of the model and raises ModelNotFoundError otherwise (e.g. after an upgrade that changed the model's outputs); it does not fetch older code or weights (weights are pinned per revision by URL and SHA-256). To reproduce a run, pin the package and the revision together: pip install fastforks==<version> and stereo.load("las2-s@1"); fastforks info MODEL shows the revision, weight URLs and SHA-256.

Pin a deployment: (1) pip install fastforks==<version>; (2) load model@rev; (3) record fastforks list --format json (weights_sha256 per model) as the lock record; (4) fastforks download MODEL --check verifies the files offline; (5) set FASTFORKS_OFFLINE=1 in production.

Options

fastforks info MODEL lists a model's load options with their validated defaults, e.g. the number of refinement iterations:

from fastforks import stereo

model = stereo.load("raft-stereo-middlebury", options={"iters": 16})
result = model("left.png", "right.png")
result.options  # {"iters": 16}: non-default options are recorded in every result

One name per concept across families; the old (upstream) names are accepted as aliases (giving both is an OptionsError):

ConceptOptionOld names
Longer side of the network input, pxlong_sideprocess_res (Depth Anything 3), processing_res (Marigold), resolution (MapAnything)
Shorter side (lower bound) of the network input, pxshort_sideinput_size (Depth Anything V2)
Side of a square with the network input's area, pxarea_sideresolution (VGGT-Omega)
Resolution level 0 to 9 (not pixels)resolution_level
Recurrent refinement iterationsiters
Diffusion denoising stepssteps

Options are checked at load (OptionsError) against the bounds and choices on the card, the same ones fastforks info MODEL and the model pages list (e.g. MoGe resolution_level 0 to 9). Options marked "speed only" (cuda_graphs) give the same results up to floating-point rounding, "precision only" (fp16_accumulate) trades accuracy for speed; all others change the outputs.

What a model takes and returns, without loading weights: depth.model_card("moge-2-vitl-normal").contract() lists the inputs (required, optional or unused: e.g. intrinsics, depth_range, prompts), the outputs with units and pixel / camera conventions, the options with their bounds, the dtypes per mode and device (implemented and validated), and what an export contains (stages inside and outside the graph, dynamic sizes); .to_dict() gives plain JSON-ready data. Intrinsics of every task use OpenCV pixel centres (see Pixel coordinates); contract().camera says so.

Licences and commercial use

fastforks separates three things; none of this is legal advice.

  • Code is installed per licence class: pip install fastforks-core has the models with permissive code, fastforks-core[nc] (and fastforks) adds non-commercial and copyleft (GPL) code. Our own code and kernels are Apache-2.0. Permissive code alone does not allow commercial use: some of these models have non-commercial weights (see below).
  • Weights are never shipped. They are downloaded from the authors' hosts (for a few models a mirror of the same files) at pinned revisions and checked against a SHA-256, so the weights licence belongs to the authors, not to fastforks. Weights with a non-commercial licence are only downloaded with FASTFORKS_NONCOMMERCIAL=1, in every install (LicenceError otherwise); local copies (weights=PATH, FASTFORKS_WEIGHTS_PATH, the cache) always load.
  • Every variant has an effective commercial status that needs the code AND the weights licence to allow commercial use: yes, no (the code or weights licence forbids it) or unclear (a custom licence, treat as no). The training data does not change the status, it is listed next to it: datasets with research-only, unclear or unstated terms are a caveat you should read (whether weights inherit them is legally unsettled). Weights without a licence of their own are assumed to carry the code licence. The model pages list the status and add a licence note where the reason is not obvious (inherited non-commercial terms, unclear dataset terms).
# needs: pip install "fastforks-core[nc]"
import fastforks
from fastforks import stereo

fastforks.list_models(commercial="yes")  # all tasks
fastforks.stereo.list_models(commercial="unclear")  # one task
stereo.model_card("foundationstereo-vit-s").licence_notes
print(stereo.model_card("hitnet-eth3d"))  # readable summary: licences and commercial status per variant
print(fastforks.describe_models(stereo.list_models("hitnet*")))  # table: licences, commercial, what blocks a "yes"

The flag is decided by the code and weights licences only. GPL code counts as yes (with copyleft obligations: see fastforks info MODEL); training data is a note, not part of the flag.

Most variants are yes; the others are no or unclear (fastforks list --commercial no shows them). A yes can still depend on training data with research-only or unstated terms, or on weights whose licence is only assumed from the code: check fastforks info MODEL (licence notes) before shipping.

Already have the weights?

from fastforks import stereo

model = stereo.load("igev-stereo-sceneflow", weights="runs/igev_finetuned.pth")  # your own weights, e.g. a fine-tune
  • weights=PATH: the file, or for a variant with several files (e.g. Marigold's diffusers layout) a directory that holds them as <dir>/<name>; for weights shipped inside an archive, the extracted file. It must have the same file format, keys and shapes as the original. It is not hash-checked, so the reference checks of the model id no longer apply (one WARNING log line says so; model.weights holds the files and the model's repr shows them), but it is loaded strictly: missing, unexpected or reshaped keys raise CheckpointMismatchError (a WeightsError) listing them, and a missing or unreadable file (another format, empty, truncated) a WeightsError naming it. Floating-point tensors in another precision than the original (e.g. a float32 fine-tune of Depth Pro's float16 checkpoint) are cast to the model's.
  • labels= (classification): classification.load("resnet50", weights="ft.pth", labels=my_1000_names) names the classes of a fine-tuned head (a list of non-empty strings, in logit order, one per logit: 1000 for resnet50, else OptionsError, checked before loading; the head size is the family's, fixed). Only the names change (result.class_names, top()); the input handling and what the logits mean stay the family's. Fine-tunes with another number of classes do not load (the head shape is checked): build that model in timm / torchvision with your head and speed it up with fastforks.patch.
  • FASTFORKS_WEIGHTS_PATH: directories (os.pathsep-separated) holding the original files as <dir>/<family>/<file> or <dir>/<file> (e.g. a shared network drive); they are used in place and hash-checked, a copy that does not match is skipped.
  • Hugging Face hub cache: weights hosted on Hugging Face (huggingface.co/<repo>/resolve/<rev>/<file>) are taken from HF_HUB_CACHE (else the older HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE, else HF_HOME/hub, else ~/.cache/huggingface/hub) if a snapshot there matches the recorded SHA-256; the torch hub cache (TORCH_HOME/hub/checkpoints, else ~/.cache/torch/hub/checkpoints) likewise by file name. Both are only read; a copy that does not match, or a cache directory that cannot be read, is skipped and the file is downloaded.
  • fastforks download MODEL (--kernels for the kernel binaries) fetches everything into the user cache ahead of time, e.g. before going offline. A model that fails (e.g. gated without a token) does not stop the others: it is listed as MISSING ... at the end and the command exits 1. --arch sm_89 fetches the binaries of a GPU you do not have, --check verifies the cache without network (a file whose size and mtime match its recorded stamp is not re-hashed), --dry-run lists the download size (the archive, once) and licence classes. FASTFORKS_OFFLINE=1 (or HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1) forbids every download; a missing file then raises an error naming it and the command that fetches it. For containers see Docker images. fastforks download --kernels-only --all-archs fetches every kernel binary (~240 MiB; one GPU target ~34 MiB) without weights; the files land in FASTFORKS_CACHE (default: the platform user cache, ~/.cache/fastforks on Linux). The cache is content-addressed (blobs/sha256/<ab>/<sha256>), so a copy of it is not a FASTFORKS_KERNEL_PATH: that wants the manifest's file names, <dir>/<lib>/<lib>-<hash>-<arch>.fatbin (or .so; <dir>/<name> also works), e.g. kernels/fs/fs-f6f8de2cca1e-sm_80.fatbin (names: fastforks/kernels/<lib>/manifest.toml). fastforks download --kernels --arch sm_80 prints <lib>-<hash>:<arch>: <cache path> per file; copy each path to that name. Files are hash-checked on use. To move everything instead, copy the whole cache and set FASTFORKS_CACHE to the copy (with FASTFORKS_OFFLINE=1 it may be read-only). --check verifies offline.

Inputs and outputs

  • Images: file paths, PIL images, numpy arrays (HWC / BHWC, RGB; convert OpenCV's BGR first) and torch tensors (CHW / BCHW). Integer images are scaled by their dtype's maximum; float images must be in [0, 1].
  • Paths are a convenience for standard images (PNG, JPEG, BMP, WebP, 8/16-bit grayscale TIFF / PNG), read with Pillow. Files Pillow would read lossily (16-bit colour PNG / TIFF, float or 32-bit integer images) raise InputError. For anything else (scientific TIFF, EXR, raw, .npy, OpenCV), load it yourself and pass a numpy array (HWC, RGB; e.g. cv2.imread(path, cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED) then BGR to RGB, uint16 or float in [0, 1]) or a torch tensor (CHW).
  • Files are read as stored: an EXIF orientation tag (phone photos) is not applied, so the pixels (and SAM prompt coordinates) are the stored, possibly rotated ones; one WARNING per process names the first such file. For an upright photo pass ImageOps.exif_transpose(Image.open(path)). CMYK / YCbCr JPEGs: pass Image.open(path).convert("RGB").
  • Classifiers resize the shorter side (to resize, e.g. 256) and centre-crop (crop, e.g. 224), so content near the border is cut off; probabilities are a softmax over the model's fixed label set (not calibrated, they sum to 1 even for an image of no class). Steps, as data_config lists them: float image in [0, 1] resized with torch (antialiased, the card's interpolation), centre crop, mean / std normalisation. The original PIL uint8 resize (and so timm.data.create_transform(**model.data_config) on a PIL image) gives different pixels: logits can move by ~0.5 and close top-5 ranks can swap. Compare against timm with the same float tensor input, not a PIL image.
  • MoGe intrinsics=: used only as the focal length fx; fy within 1 % of fx and a principal point within 5 % of the centre, else InputError. Use the result's intrinsics (the camera the points really use) afterwards.
  • Segmentation labels: class 0 is a class like any other (ADE20K wall), there is no ignore / background mask.
  • Grayscale (HW, 1HW, mode L) and RGBA images are accepted and converted to RGB (grayscale is repeated to three channels, alpha is dropped).
  • Stereo pairs are not checked for swapped left / right images: the result is finite but wrong (disparity is x_left - x_right, so pass the left camera's image first).
  • Prompt points outside the image are accepted as given (as upstream SAM does); boxes (x0, y0, x1, y1) with x1 < x0 or y1 < y0 raise InputError.
  • Embedding search (features): pooler_output is not unit-length and every image must have the same size, for the gallery and the queries alike (the size changes the embedding):
    import torch.nn.functional as F

g = F.normalize(model(gallery_images).pooler_output, dim=-1)  # [N, D]; same-size images, one batched call
q = F.normalize(model(query_images).pooler_output, dim=-1)  # same size as the gallery
scores = q @ g.T  # cosine similarity [Q, N]; scores.topk(5, dim=-1) for the best matches
  • Lists are not batches: stack same-size images into one array or tensor (multi-view models take a list of views).
  • Any size above the model's minimum: resizing or padding to what the network needs and back happen inside the call, so dense maps (disparity, depth, labels) have the input's resolution. Classifiers resize and crop as the model expects.
  • Batches: pass [B, 3, H, W] tensors (or BHWC arrays) to get [B, H, W] maps ([B, classes] logits).
  • Exceptions to batching: detection returns a list of DetectionResult (one per image); promptable segmentation calls take one image (batch the image encoder with get_image_embeddings, then prompt per image); multi-view models take the N views of one scene as the leading dimension (not independent images). Stereo, depth, classification, segmentation and features return tensors with a leading B.
  • Outputs are tensors on the model's device; result.numpy() returns them as a dict of NumPy arrays by name (None fields left out, extras flattened in, bfloat16 as float32). Some models also return result.confidence or result.extras (see the model page).
  • Results are snapshots you own: frozen dataclasses with new tensors per call (never buffers a later call reuses, also with CUDA graphs). .to(device) / .cpu() return new results. numpy() arrays of CPU tensors share their memory; arrays of cached values (calibrated stereo depth(), run_many's numpy maps, rig matrices) are read-only: .copy() to edit.

Pixel coordinates

Intrinsics, cameras and rigs (depth, multi-view, stereo) use OpenCV pixel centres and axes: the top-left pixel's centre is (0, 0), the image centre ((W - 1) / 2, (H - 1) / 2), x right, y down, z forward, cam_to_world maps camera to world. Models whose original code uses another grid are converted inside. From a corner-origin matrix (COLMAP, MoGe, nerfstudio): cx_colmap = cx_opencv + 0.5 (same for cy); read_calib(..., "colmap") does it for you.

Saving maps

save exists on results that hold dense maps: stereo, depth, multi-view, segmentation (labels) and promptable segmentation (masks); classification, features and detection results have none (use result.numpy() or the fields). result.save(path) writes the primary map (disparity, depth or inverse_depth, labels, masks; key="confidence" or an extras name picks another) as one [H, W] file; the suffix selects the format, and an unknown suffix raises with the list this result accepts. Batches are not split (pass one image per call; leading dimensions of size 1 are dropped; for several masks write one, fastforks.save("m.png", r.masks[i])); a multi-view result with several views takes view= (the input view index). .npy and .png keep integer and bool maps exact (their dtype); fastforks.save of a result without save raises and names the arrays to np.save. A calibrated stereo result's .tif / .npy / .pfm hold the depth (key="disparity" for the disparity) and its .png the KITTI disparity. Maps are written as they are: invalid pixels keep their finite values, so mask them first (np.where(result.valid(), depth, np.nan); depth results: their mask). A .tif carries one ImageDescription tag (model, map, kind / unit). torch.save(result, path) works; torch.load(path) in a fresh process needs the result's class imported first (e.g. from fastforks.classification import ClassificationResult; importing fastforks.<task> is enough), and an ImageEmbeddings also torch.serialization.safe_globals([ImageEmbeddings]) (or weights_only=False for your own files). Result tensors are inference tensors: .clone() one before an in-place edit.

suffixcontent
.tif / .tifffloat32 TIFF, deflate + floating-point predictor; opens in tifffile, OpenCV, Pillow, GDAL
.npyraw float32; bool and integer maps (labels, masks) keep their dtype (bool, int64, ...)
.pfmraw float32, bottom row first (Middlebury)
.pnginteger and bool maps (labels, masks): 1-bit for bool, 8-bit for 0..255, 16-bit for 0..65535; float maps are refused, except a stereo disparity or a depth result (depth, inverse_depth): uint16, value x 256, 0 = invalid, clipped at 255.996 (KITTI convention; metric depth keeps 1/256 m) (run_many / stereo run with rig= write depth: not .png)
.ply, .las / .lazpoint clouds: stereo with rig=, multi-view (all views merged; without world_points: depth unprojected with intrinsics and cam_to_world, header units: those of the given cam_to_world), depth results with points or metric depth + intrinsics (the finite points inside mask), coloured; see below

Point clouds (.ply, .las / .laz) are metric in OpenCV axes (x right, y down, z forward) unless axes= says otherwise:

  • axes= (stereo, depth, multi-view results and fastforks.save): "opencv" (default, RDF), "opengl" / "blender" (RUB), "ros" (FLU), "pytorch3d" (LUF) or any 3-letter code with one of R/L, U/D, F/B (the directions of x, y, z), e.g. "RFU"; anything else raises OptionsError listing the presets. The PLY header comments (and the LAS VLR, system id fastforks) name the version, units, axes, frame and the pixel convention. A LAS / LAZ is a local frame without CRS.
  • max_depth= (metres, z in OpenCV axes) drops points beyond it; the default keeps every finite point. There is no other masking: stereo points are the finite ones, depth and multi-view clouds keep the model's mask.
  • Colours: stereo uses the rectified image; depth and multi-view results colour from the input image they were called with (the result keeps a reference, no copy). A metric depth result without points but with intrinsics (e.g. da3metric) writes its unprojected depth; without intrinsics call the model with intrinsics=K.
  • A multi-view result saves the merged, masked cloud of all views in the world frame; view= writes one view; save_scene writes cameras, images and points as a COLMAP or nerfstudio scene (below).
  • Unposed multi-view models (no cam_to_world= given) use the frame of view 0 as the world; cam_to_world is OpenCV camera-to-world. For MapAnything world_points is the primary output; depth + intrinsics + cam_to_world is its pinhole approximation (intrinsics are fitted to the predicted rays), so they differ slightly; its metric_scale is in extras.

To COLMAP / nerfstudio: r.save_scene(folder, "colmap") writes the views' input images losslessly (images/frame_00001.png, numbered by input view; image_names= references your own files, relative to folder) and a text model in sparse/0 (PINHOLE, pixel centres at +0.5, world-to-camera poses, points without tracks); "nerfstudio" writes transforms.json (camera-to-world in OpenGL axes, cx / cy +0.5) and sparse_pc.ply. The points are the masked points of all views, at most max_points=100_000 (fixed seed); both formats can share one folder.

python examples/simple_trainer.py default --data_dir scene --data_factor 1  # gsplat
ns-train splatfacto --data scene  # nerfstudio: reads transforms.json and sparse_pc.ply

Colored PNG for viewing (numpy only; matplotlib.cm works too if installed):

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

d = result.disparity.cpu().numpy()  # or result.depth() with rig=, inverse_depth for depth
ok = np.isfinite(d)
t = np.zeros_like(d)
t[ok] = (d[ok] - d[ok].min()) / max(np.ptp(d[ok]), 1e-9)
stops = np.array([[68, 1, 84], [59, 82, 139], [33, 145, 140], [94, 201, 98], [253, 231, 37]], float)  # viridis
rgb = np.stack([np.interp(t, np.linspace(0, 1, 5), stops[:, c]) for c in range(3)], -1).astype(np.uint8)
rgb[~ok] = 0
Image.fromarray(rgb).save("depth_color.png")
# label map (segmentation): result.save("labels.png") (8-bit up to 255 classes, else 16-bit) or result.save("labels.npy")

A TIFF is about 1.9x smaller than raw float32 and bit-exact. bits=10 first rounds the mantissa to 10 bits (relative error at most 2**-11, 0.05 % for normal floats; values that would overflow or flush to 0 stay exact) and gives 7-10x; any bits in 1..23 works. Writing takes about 5-15 ms for a 1.4 MP map (strips are compressed in parallel with isal; without it the standard zlib writes the same file more slowly).

result.save("disparity.tif")  # lossless
result.save("disparity.tif", bits=10)  # 7-10x smaller than raw, error <= 0.05 %

Video and repeated sizes

Keep the model and the frame size fixed. The first call at a new size is slower (memory planning, cuDNN plans), so warm up at each size before timing: 4 calls for kernels models that replay CUDA graphs (Fast-ACVNet, CoEx, LAS2, RT-MonSter++), 1-2 for the others. Stereo models also have model.run_many(lefts, rights) for a stream of pairs; it returns a pipeline that starts working at once, a bounded prefetch pairs ahead (with save_to=, files may appear before the first iteration). Iterate it (for r in ..., or list(...) with save_to=) to drain it; to stop early use with model.run_many(...) as p: for r in p: ... or p.close() (it finishes the writes in progress and drops the other queued pairs); a plain break does not close a pipeline that is still referenced. Outputs for the same input are bitwise equal between calls and processes, except portable CoEx and Fast-ACVNet on CUDA (differences of 1-3 px on single pixels; set torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True to remove them, at about 5 % speed). Batched calls can differ from single calls in the last bits.

Several GPUs

portable runs on any device: stereo.load(..., device="cuda:1"). kernels uses one CUDA device per process (the kernels are bound to one context); a second device in the same process raises BackendUnavailableError. Use one process per GPU.

Threads

Deployment: CUDA and MPS calls take one process-wide lock and kernels binds one CUDA device per process, so run models in parallel (or one per GPU) as separate processes.

Calls from several threads give the same outputs as single-threaded calls. Load every model before other threads start calling models.

casebehaviour
one model, several threadscalls run one at a time (a model is not reentrant)
CUDA calls of different modelsone at a time per process (one process-wide lock), so a pipeline of models in threads does not overlap on the GPU: use one process per model
MPS calls of different modelsone at a time per process (the same lock: PyTorch's MPS backend is not thread-safe)
CPU calls of different modelsrun in parallel
a model called inside another model's callallowed (the lock is reentrant)
CUDA streamscalls run on the caller's current stream (with torch.cuda.stream(s):), also TensorRTEngine; synchronise that stream before reading outputs on another one
deviceskernels: one CUDA device per process (see above)

Running on the CPU

device="cpu" runs the portable backend in float32. On a Ryzen 7 5800X (8 threads) fastforks is 1.0-2.2x faster than the original code. Set torch.set_num_threads(n) before the first call to the cores you really have (in a container, os.cpu_count() shows the host's). Going from 1 to 8 threads gives about 4x on large networks and 2x on small ones. Kernels need CUDA. Tested on x86-64 only; on a Mac, use the GPU (next section).

Apple silicon (MPS)

On a Mac without CUDA, load puts a model on the Apple GPU (mps) when its family is validated there, else on the CPU; result.backend.device says which. Every family is validated except those with gated weights (DINOv3, DINOv3-ConvNeXt, SAM 3, VGGT-Omega). device="mps" also runs those, unvalidated: an op MPS lacks raises. On MPS kernels exists for RAFT-Stereo, the IGEV family (IGEV-Stereo, Selective-IGEV, GREAT-IGEV, IGEV++, MoCha-Stereo, MonSter, MonSter++), CFNet, LiteAnyStereo V2 (LaS2), HITNet, AANet, CREStereo, NMRF, BridgeDepth, DEFOM-Stereo and FoundationStereo: Metal kernels for each family's hot spot (ConvGRUs, correlation and geometry lookups, cost volumes, HITNet's warp costs, AANet's deformable sampling), float16, and for MoGe-3 (its sparse convolutions) and VGGT (the aggregator's q / k LayerNorm and RoPE) in float32. They compile on the device in under a second on first use; mode="auto" picks it. Every other family runs portable.

  • dtype: float32 by default. dtype="float16" works where the card lists it (fastforks info MODEL, row apple gpu). It saves memory (up to half) and on an M1 Pro is also faster: median 1.15x over 60 models, up to 2.9x on memory-bound stereo cost volumes (GREAT-IGEV, CoEx, CAS-GwcNet), rarely slower (HITNet, Mask2Former 0.94x).
  • A few small steps run on the CPU or in float32 by design: float64 maths in MoGe and SAM, one adaptive pooling in S2M2, Depth Anything 3's bicubic resize.
  • The first call at a new input size takes 0.5-4 s longer (PyTorch compiles the Metal kernels for that shape).
  • MPS shares the host RAM (no separate GPU memory); the MPS memory in the benchmarks is the process's peak footprint (Activity Monitor). A model larger than the free RAM swaps (slower, but it runs); keep several GB free on the system disk, since with a full disk swapping can freeze the machine.

torch.compile, torch.export, ONNX and TensorRT

Every model has model.module(), the traceable part of the portable model (what it covers per task: API; stereo and depth include scaling, padding, network and cropping) as an nn.Module (inputs and outputs as the task's runner takes and returns them; see the API pages): for stereo RGB [B, 3, H, W] float32 in [0, 1] for both views in, disparity [B, H, W] float32 out; depth one image in, its main map out. Call it under torch.inference_mode(). ONNX and TensorRT export and TensorRTEngine work the same way for every task.

import torch

from fastforks import stereo

model = stereo.load("igev-stereo-sceneflow", mode="portable")
module = model.module()
compiled = torch.compile(module, fullgraph=True)
program = torch.export.export(module, model.example_inputs(384, 1248))

A kernels model called inside your own torch.compiled function is a graph break: the kernels run eagerly, the code around them is compiled. TorchScript (torch.jit.trace / script) is not supported (deprecated upstream): use torch.export of the portable module(); kernels-patched models (load(mode="kernels"), patch) do not export.

Or keep the high-level API and compile in place (kernels raises BackendUnavailableError), or export:

model.compile()  # every task call now runs compiled; again with other arguments replaces it
model.export_onnx("m.onnx", 384, 1248)
model.export_tensorrt("m.engine", 384, 1248)  # on the target GPU; then stereo.TensorRTEngine("m.engine")(left, right)

# needs: pip install "fastforks-core[nc]" "fastforks-core[onnx]"
# S2M2's code and weights are non-commercial: its weights download only with FASTFORKS_NONCOMMERCIAL=1
fastforks export s2m2-s --format onnx --size 384x1248          # float32 ONNX of the portable backend
fastforks export s2m2-s --format trt --fp16 --size 704x1280    # stereo / depth / segmentation / detection need --size; engine + check
fastforks export depth-anything-v2-s --format trt --fp16 --size 518x770

From Python: model.export_onnx(path[, height, width]) and model.export_tensorrt(path[, height, width]); run an engine with stereo.TensorRTEngine(path)(left, right) (depth.TensorRTEngine(path)(image)). Exports have one fixed size and batch by default (size ranges: see export); the size must lie in model.size_range() (stereo, depth, segmentation and detection have no default size; classification and features default to model.export_size()). A TensorRT engine only runs on the GPU model and TensorRT version it was built with: build it on the target machine. Install the exporters with pip install "fastforks-core[onnx]" / "fastforks-core[tensorrt]". See export for inputs and outputs per task, what works per model and how TensorRT compares with kernels.

Patching your own timm / torchvision / transformers model

fastforks.patch(model, mode="auto") speeds up a classifier you built yourself (weights loaded) in place and returns a FastModel (fp32 NCHW in and out; .backend, .report, .original). base_type(module) returns the class a patched module had before the override. Both are for models outside the fastforks registry; the registry models use load.

Rewritten: timm / torchvision CNNs (ResNet, RegNet, EfficientNet, MobileNetV2-V4, DenseNet, VGG, ShuffleNetV2, ...), ConvNeXt, Swin, timm ViT Block (packed qkv), EvaBlock and HF SiglipEncoderLayer (the full list: fastforks._optimize.COVERED). Anything else (e.g. HF ViTModel, Dinov2Model) only gets BatchNorm folding, the dtype cast and channels-last: patch logs a WARNING saying so, and mode="kernels" raises. A patched model's device and dtype are fixed by patch (.half() / .to() raise, by design): patch a copy.deepcopy of the original again for another device or dtype. Modules with forward or backward hooks are not rewritten (their hooks keep running; mode="kernels" refuses such a model). Activations run channels-last (CUDA, and CNNs on the CPU): in a forward that torch.fx cannot trace, a .view() of a conv output can raise; use .reshape() or .flatten().

Training and gradients

fastforks is for inference. Task calls (model(x)) run without autograd. For gradients use the portable backend: load(..., mode="portable").module() and a patch(model, mode="portable") model are plain PyTorch (eval mode, BatchNorm folded) and backpropagate to the input and the weights. kernels have no backward: a FastModel in kernels mode raises for an input that requires grad, and module() raises BackendUnavailableError. Train the original model; patch modifies it in place, so patch a copy. A fine-tuned module() state dict loads back with load(..., weights=) (the module() key prefix is accepted), except classification, whose module() has folded BatchNorm: fine-tune the timm / torchvision model and pass its state_dict file as weights=.

Serving (web service, batch worker)

  • One model per process and GPU: calls hold a process-wide lock, so threads add no throughput; scale with processes (load the model inside each worker, see Processes below) or one process per GPU.
  • Warm up before the first request, at the sizes you serve: one call with a real image or torch.rand(1, 3, height, width) (images are in [0, 1]; example_inputs are normalised, for export only); the first call at a new size runs eagerly (and with kernels captures graphs).
  • Cap the input size yourself (e.g. resize to a few buckets): one 48 MP upload keeps the reserved GPU memory high (allocator cache); torch.cuda.empty_cache() after such a request gives it back.
  • Map errors to HTTP: InputError / ArgumentError (bad image, bad keyword) to 4xx, other FastforksError subclasses (WeightsError, BackendUnavailableError, ...) to 5xx; one except fastforks.FastforksError covers all.
  • Images as uploaded bytes: pass bytes, bytearray or io.BytesIO of the encoded file; corrupt data raises InputError.

Notes for deployments

Per-frame loop (mono depth, detection, classification): load once, warm up at the frame size, then call per frame. There is no run_many and no folder command outside stereo; for a folder of images load once and loop:

import pathlib
from fastforks import depth

model = depth.load("depth-anything-v2-s")
for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("images").glob("*.jpg")):
    model(p).save(f"out/{p.stem}.tif")

import time
from fastforks import detection

det = detection.load("rtdetrv2-s-coco")  # defaults: score >= 0.05, at most 100 boxes
det(first_frame, score_threshold=0.5)  # warm-up at the real size; the first call also captures CUDA graphs (kernels)
for frame in frames:  # numpy HWC uint8, torch or PIL; keep the size fixed, call from one thread
    boxes = det(frame, score_threshold=0.5, max_detections=30)  # per-call overrides of the load options

Memory per input size: kernels keep a cuDNN plan and a CUDA graph per input size, so a stream of many different sizes grows the reserved memory (bounded: 512 cuDNN plans, a per-model cap on graphs that evicts the stalest; the first calls at a new size run eagerly). Fixed sizes, or resizing to a few buckets, avoids it; del model; gc.collect(); torch.cuda.empty_cache() releases a model's share. Host RSS of a GPU process is mostly the CUDA / cuDNN libraries (about 1.1 GB for plain PyTorch with one conv and one GEMM, 2.3 GB for a detection model).

CPU-only install: take PyTorch's CPU wheel first (pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu), then pip install fastforks-core: the lean CPU install is about 0.9 GB on disk, mostly torch. fastforks env shows the thread count and whether torch is a CPU build.

Processes: a model cannot be pickled (it holds device memory and locks), so with multiprocessing / a Pool load the model inside each worker (initializer=), or start workers with spawn. Loading it before a fork and calling it in the child can deadlock in the CPU thread pool (libgomp); fastforks logs a warning once when a forked child calls such a model. Results pickle, and torch.save(result, path) / torch.load(path) work with the default weights_only=True.

Provenance: result.backend also carries library (the fastforks version) and weights (SHA-256 of the recorded weight files; with load(weights=PATH) see backend.checkpoint); the kernel libraries and builds are in backend.kernels.

Audits: fastforks list --format json (or csv) prints every model with its code and weights licence, commercial status and reasons, data notes, revision, weights URLs and SHA-256. FASTFORKS_COMMERCIAL_ONLY=1 makes load raise a LicenceError for every model whose status is not yes (also with weights=PATH and for cached weights) and list / list_models show only the yes models. commercial=yes includes copyleft licences (GPL): check the licence column of list / info. Weight URLs on Hugging Face are pinned to a commit; the weights of other hosts (Google Drive, Dropbox, GitHub releases) are pinned by SHA-256 only.

Kernel trust model: the kernel binaries come from our Hugging Face repo; their SHA-256 are in the manifest inside the wheel (which pip installs from PyPI) and every download is checked against it before it is loaded. There are no signatures or SBOM yet, so the wheel's integrity is the root of trust (pin it with pip --require-hashes).

Command line helpers

fastforks env prints versions, GPU and kernel binaries (paste it into bug reports); fastforks <command> --help lists every flag.

Speed check

fastforks bench igev-stereo-sceneflow                            # portable and kernels side by side, median of 10 runs
fastforks bench igev-stereo-sceneflow --mode portable --dtype float32 --size 544x960
fastforks bench depth-anything-v2-s --device cpu --size 518x518

bench works for any model, with synthetic input of the right kind (an image; a pair for stereo). It prints time and peak memory in MiB. On CUDA: "allocated" is what tensors use (weights included), "reserved" is what PyTorch's allocator holds from the driver (roughly what nvidia-smi shows for the process, without the CUDA context). On MPS it prints the Metal driver's allocation (GPU buffers only); on the CPU no memory.

Tiers

fastforks list shows a tier per model: stable (tested and measured), experimental (works, less tested) or deprecated (kept for old code, will be removed). --tier filters by it.

Troubleshooting

  • BackendUnavailableError / KernelUnavailableError: mode="kernels" cannot run here. The message names the reason (GPU too old, no binary, driver). mode="auto" falls back to portable instead. fastforks env shows the binaries your GPU would use.
  • A kernel or weight download fails: check the network, or fetch ahead with fastforks download MODEL --kernels and copy the cache (see Docker images). FASTFORKS_OFFLINE=1 forbids downloads.
  • Gated weights (for example VGGT-Omega, DINOv3): fastforks never handles your Hugging Face token; gated downloads go through huggingface_hub (pip install huggingface_hub). Accept the licence on the model's Hugging Face page, log in (hf auth login, or huggingface_hub.login() in Python), then load again. By hand: hf download <repo> <file> --revision <rev> (the error prints it) puts the file in the hub cache, or use a copy on FASTFORKS_WEIGHTS_PATH or weights=PATH.
  • CUDA out of memory: use a smaller input, mode="portable" (often less memory), or release_graphs() on models that replay CUDA graphs. fastforks info MODEL shows the largest size tested.
  • A model fails in load naming a missing package: install the extra it names, for example fastforks-core[transformers].
